The Counterpoise Lines: a story bible

Drevast is a country that stands on its end. It fills the Karrow cleft, a gash in the mountains eighty kilometres long and seldom more than five across, and its people have never agreed whether they are the last settlers of the lowlands or the first of the sky. At the bottom, three hundred and fifty metres above the sea, the Sill river leaves the cleft and spreads into the grain flats around the port of Pannock. At the top, twenty-three hundred metres higher, the town of Ostrel sits on a shelf of rock that the maps call the Shelf and the people call the Lid. Almost nothing grows on the Lid except barley, wool and stubbornness, and almost nothing can be made there without things that come from below: salt, iron, lamp oil, medicine, glass, seed, paper, brides. The only way up is the Ladder. The Ladder is a chain of seven cableways, each a separate line with its own pair of cars, stacked end to end so that the top station of one line is the bottom station of the next. Nobody walks it who can ride, and nobody rides it who has not first been weighed.

The premise of the novel is arithmetic. Everything that goes up the Ladder is lifted by water coming down. No steam engine, no horse and no wheel turned by a man drives any line of it; the cars are moved by the weight of the water they carry, and all of that water begins in one place, a mountain lake above Ostrel called the Brimmer, which is fed by one dying glacier, Old Mara. The Ladder was designed in a century that took the glacier for a fact of the landscape, like the cleft itself, and nobody drew up a plan for the day it might not be there. So long as the Brimmer is full, the country is a clever machine. When the Brimmer thins, the country thins with it, from the top down, and the book follows the people who notice that first and the people who prefer not to. It is a story about a shortage, but it is not told as a disaster. Nothing in Drevast explodes. Things simply arrive a little later each year, cost a little more, and are carried by people who have a little less to give, until one summer the Lid is truly a lid and the town beneath it must decide what to be.

A line works as a seesaw works, except that this seesaw is a kilometre and a half long and stood on its end. Two cars hang from one haul-rope, which loops over a great iron wheel called the Great Sheave in the upper station and around a smaller return wheel in the lower, so that when one car is at the top the other is at the bottom. Under the floor of every car hangs a steel tank called a belly, which is the car's ballast. A belly holds ninety barrels of water when it is filled to the Mark, and the Mark is a ring of white paint inside the tank that fixes the most water it may ever take. At the top station the belly of the waiting car is filled from the feed channel, so that car is now heavier than its partner, which waits at the bottom with an empty belly and a deck loaded with freight or passengers. The margin by which the heavy car outweighs the light one is called the counterpoise, and a line moves only while its counterpoise is positive. Once the brakemen ease the Sheave, the heavy car sinks, the rope runs and the light car rises. At the bottom the belly is opened and its water runs into the tailrace, a stone channel that falls by its own weight to the top station of the next line down, where another belly is waiting to be filled.

Water is weighed, and so is everything else. The Commission counts in tallies, and a tally is the weight of one barrel of water, which makes a full belly worth ninety tallies of ballast. Friction, the weight of the rope and the down-freight that rides in the heavy car all eat into that, so in a clean season a ninety-barrel belly lifts about sixty tallies of load, a ratio the wrights state as two for three. The draw of a line is the number of tallies it lifts in a working day, and the working day runs from the dawn bell to the dusk bell, twelve hours by the Ostrel clock. A line that manages thirty runs in a day, with sixty tallies on each, has a draw of eighteen hundred, and eighteen hundred is the figure that the Commission's ledgers treat as a good day on the Seventh Line. Passengers are weighed at the gate and charged by the tally; a grown man is about half a tally, a child a little under a quarter, and an Ostrel bride with her trunk is entered separately as freight, which is a joke the book makes once and then drops.

The same water works seven times. A barrel loaded into a belly at Ostrel descends the Seventh Line, spills into the tailrace at Saddle Gate, fills a belly of the Sixth, and so on down the cleft until what remains of it enters the Sill at Pannock and turns the lowland mills. Every middle station is built in two tiers, the lower yard of the line above standing about twelve metres higher than the upper yard of the line below, so that the tailrace falls by its own weight and needs no pump. Water is lost at every hand-over to seepage, splash, evaporation and frost, roughly four barrels in a hundred, which means that of every hundred barrels loaded at Ostrel about seventy-eight reach the First Line, and that on a day when the Seventh manages thirty runs the First manages perhaps twenty-three. The arithmetic has two consequences that drive the plot. First, the lowest lines are always the thirstiest, so the First Line is the first to run short in any bad year. Second, a stall travels down the Ladder at the speed of water: when a line stops, the line below it receives nothing until the stoppage is cleared, and its dispatcher learns of the trouble not by telegraph but by the silence in the tailrace.

The Brimmer is a tarn of dark, very cold water about two kilometres above the town, held in a bowl of rock and old moraine and closed at its lower lip by a stone dam three hundred years older than the Ladder. It holds forty thousand barrels when full, which is less than a lowland brewery uses in a season, and that is the first thing visitors fail to believe. It does not need to be larger because it is never meant to be still. Old Mara, the glacier that hangs above it in the last cirque of the Karrow, delivers melt from May to September, and the Brimmer's outflow, the Sluice, is cut open at dawn and closed at dusk. In a normal year the Sluice passes more water than the lake holds, again and again, so that the Brimmer works as a gate rather than a store. Its level is read twice daily from a gauge-post at Tarn House, the small stone station on the east shore where the Commission's hydrographers live, and the reading, called the Brimmer figure, is telegraphed to every dispatcher in the cleft before the dawn bell. If the figure is high, the day is long. If it is low, the Commission decides what each line is allowed to do with it.

The stations, from the bottom, are Pannock, Tuck Hollow, Orrel Crossing, Ketterby, Greyfall, Cinder Rest, Saddle Gate and Ostrel, and the seven lines run between them in order: the First Line from Pannock to Tuck Hollow, the Second to Orrel Crossing, the Third to Ketterby, the Fourth to Greyfall, the Fifth to Cinder Rest, the Sixth to Saddle Gate and the Seventh to Ostrel. Every station is more than a platform. Tuck Hollow is a market town built of freight sheds, Orrel Crossing is where the Sill is bridged and the road to the eastern pastures leaves the cleft, and Ketterby is a cheese town whose caves hold the cold. Greyfall sits almost exactly halfway up, in a basin of grey scree that gives it its name, and for that reason it holds the wrights' yard, the dispatch school and the brake sheds that serve the middle of the Ladder. Cinder Rest is a bare ledge with a hostel on it. Saddle Gate guards the narrow neck below the Lid and is the coldest of the stations after dark. One fact about the ordering is worth keeping in mind: the lines are numbered from the bottom, in the order they were built, but the water runs from the top, so the First Line is the oldest of the seven and the last to be served.

Every line hangs on a single haul-rope of sedgewire, and sedgewire is a rope of twelve steel strands braided around a core of treated sedge fibre. The steel carries the load. The sedge is there to listen, in the wrights' phrase: it damps the rope's shiver, keeps the strands from biting one another, and holds water like a wick, so that a sound rope is always faintly damp at the heart. The sedge is cut in the marshes below Pannock, retted for a season and braided on the long walks at Greyfall, where the Ombrecht family has made rope since before the Ladder was finished. A new rope for a line costs about what Ostrel spends on bread in a month, which is the reason for the rule that a haul-rope is retired after seven years of service, however it looks. Seven years is not a measurement of wear. It is a promise that the wrights make to the dispatchers, and the dispatchers make to everyone else, so that nobody has to look at a rope that seems fine and decide on the day whether to trust it. A retired rope is not thrown away; it becomes bridge cable and well-rope in the lowlands, a second life that keeps the wrights solvent and the rule honest.

Two further customs turn the machine into a discipline. The first is the Pass, a short stretch of double track in the middle of every line where the two cars meet and swing by each other; a Pass is a place, and the person who works it is the Pass-keeper. On every run both cars halt at the Pass for one full minute, called the Held Minute, while the keeper lays a hand on the rope and listens to it and checks that the bands are cool. Since the cars share a rope, one halting means both halt, and for that minute everyone aboard hangs in the open air above the cleft with nothing to do but think about it. The second custom is the two-key rule: a line may not start until the dispatcher's key has been turned at the dispatch desk and the inspector's key has been turned at the brake house, both in the same minute. The two people who turn those keys, one who counts the weight and one who answers for the brakes, are called a pair, and a pair is posted together to a station for years. By long habit they know each other's silences. The book is built around one such pair.

Daily life on the Ladder has a rhythm that the book uses as scenery. The dawn bell opens the day and the dusk bell closes it; there is no night traffic, officially. Freight and people queue at every station in the dark and are weighed on the gate scales, each figure chalked on the wall by a weigher whose job is thought honest in the cleft and pitiless everywhere else. On the first day of every month, called Haul Day, freight outranks passengers and the Commission lets the carts run the whole length of the cleft without stopping; on all other days the order is reversed and passengers go first. Children ride free until the age of seven, for the old reason that a child weighs almost nothing and has no say in the matter. Dogs ride at half fare and are weighed too, on principle. The highest fare on the Ladder, from Pannock to Ostrel, is paid by the tally, and a rich man in Ostrel who is heavy is thought to have been unlucky in his appetite, whereas a poor man who is heavy is assumed to have been lucky in his carrying. Superstition clings to the Held Minute: travellers hold their breath, and children are taught to count sixty.

The Highline Water Commission, always shortened to the HWC, owns the water. It was chartered in the same year that the Seventh Line opened, forty-one years before Year one, when the opening of that last line tied six older lines to a single lake and nobody could say any longer whose water was whose. The First Line had opened sixty years before Year one, and the Ladder took nineteen years to finish, which is why the Commission, not any single town, holds the Brimmer, the Sluice and every tailrace in the country. It sits in a grey building in Ostrel with a clock that is always wrong by four minutes in the Commission's favour. Its head is the Commissioner, appointed by the Assembly of Stations for a term of eight years, and the Commissioner alone holds the seal that closes the Sluice, a coil of waxed cord and a lump of red wax stamped with a ladder. The HWC employs the dispatchers, the inspectors, the weighers and the hydrographers. It does not employ the wrights, who belong to their own guild and work by contract, and that gap between the people who build the Ladder and the people who say when it may run is one of the book's small fault lines.

The Sill Freight Syndicate, the SFS, is the other power in the cleft, and it lives at the bottom. It was founded twenty-nine years before Year one by the grain carters of Pannock, who found that the Commission sold space on the First Line by the day and that any carter could be bumped at dawn by a lord's cheeses. The Syndicate's answer was to buy space in bulk, a year ahead, and resell it, and in time it controlled nearly every slot on the First Line and many on the Second. Its agents are cheerful, well fed and unembarrassed. Its quarrel with the HWC is not about whether the Ladder should run but about when, since the Commission closes the lines at dusk and a grain barge that reaches Pannock at nine in the evening is worth less by morning. The Syndicate therefore sells what the Commission forbids: the ghost car, which is a run made outside the dispatcher's book, usually after the dusk bell, with water taken from a tailrace before its proper turn. The taking is done through a thief-pipe, a hidden pipe tapped into a tailrace and plugged with a wooden bung. Ghost water is quick and cheap, and it comes out of the cisterns that the day's first runs are counting on, so the dispatcher at the next station down opens the ledger at dawn to find a cistern two hands short.

The Wrights' Guild, which has no acronym because it has never needed one, is the third body in the cleft and the only one that no authority created. It is older than the Commission and older than the Syndicate, and it began as the rope-walkers of Greyfall agreeing among themselves not to braid for anyone who would not retire a rope on time. Its charter is a single sheet. It says that a wright's seal means what the wright says it means, that a rope with a seal on it has been listened to, and that no officer of any commission may alter the meaning of a seal. The seal itself is a brass stamp pressed into a lead tag, and a wright who loses the vote of the guild loses the stamp and with it the right to be believed in public. The guild has about two hundred members, of whom perhaps twenty can truly read a rope. It pays no wages. It earns by contract, and it is therefore both poorer and freer than the people it works beside, a condition the book treats as a kind of structural honesty.

The Assembly of Stations is the country's parliament, such as it is. It has eight seats, one for each station, and meets at Ostrel in the long room above the weighing hall, where the benches are bolted to the floor so that no member can drag one toward a friend. Seats are won by the weighers and dispatchers of each station voting together, which gives the Ladder's own workers a quiet majority in the body that is supposed to oversee them and explains a good deal about its caution. It appoints the Commissioner, receives the Commission's accounts once a year, and has never in forty years refused either. It is also, by custom, the only body that may order the Commission to open its ledgers, an order it has given exactly twice and withdrawn exactly twice, each time after a delegation of dispatchers explained how many sacks of grain the audit would delay. Its members are decent, sleepy and local, and the book is careful not to make them stupid. The Assembly does not fail to act because its members are fools. It fails because every one of them depends on the Ladder for a livelihood, and a body whose members must each go home by the same cable cannot easily vote to say that the cable is in trouble.

Seven rules hold everywhere in Drevast, and every character in the book bends at least one of them. A belly is never filled past the Mark. No run begins until the dispatcher's key and the inspector's key are turned in the same minute. Both cars halt at the Pass for the Held Minute on every run, whatever the hour and whoever is aboard. A haul-rope is retired after seven years of service, however it looks. No flame is carried within thirty paces of a haul-rope, which is why Ladder smokers are a lonely and resentful class, and why a pipe is the first thing a Pass-keeper confiscates. Water is assigned, never sold, so that a station may be given a draw but may not trade it, and anyone caught selling a tally of water is guilty of the oldest offence in the Commission's code. Finally, the seal on the Sluice is broken by the Commissioner or by nobody. The rules are plain on purpose. The book's tension does not come from anyone not knowing them but from how reasonable each breach seems at the moment it is made, and from the fact that none of the seven was written to be broken by a person who meant harm.

The slow disaster is a chain of five links, and the book wants every link visible. First, Old Mara shrinks: a warmer sky melts more ice early in the season and leaves less for the end of it, so the glacier's delivery peaks sooner and falls away sooner. Second, the Brimmer, which depends on that delivery, drains below the Commission's safe figure earlier each year, and Low Day, the day in the dry stretch of the year when the lake is lowest because the harvest haul has emptied it faster than Old Mara can refill it, moves backward through the calendar. Third, the Commissioner answers a low figure by rationing the draw, cutting the number of runs each line may make, and because water works downward the cut lands hardest at the bottom of the Ladder. Fourth, grain and salt wait on the First Line, so their price in Ostrel climbs, and the climb pays for ghost cars. Fifth, ghost cars empty the cisterns that the morning runs depend on, which deepens the very shortage they were bought to relieve. At each link a decent person can say that the trouble began at the link before, and in the book several do.

The year in Drevast is cut in two by the glacier. The Fill Season runs from May to September, when Old Mara is running and the Brimmer is topped daily, and the Thin Season runs from October to April, when only the lake's springs feed it and the lines work on about a third of the summer draw. Weddings wait for June, and the wrights braid new rope in the Thin Season, when they have hands to spare. Winter has its own hazards. Ice forms in the tailraces, which boys with poles must clear, and ice on a haul-rope makes the Held Minute a dangerous one, because a rope frozen to its sheave can seize and then let go all at once. The lowland thinks the Thin Season is the dull half of the year. The Ladder knows it as the half in which accidents happen.

The cast is small by design, because the country is small and everyone in it is at most two keys, one rope and one bell away from everyone else. Eight people carry the book. Three of them are a family, the Ombrechts of Greyfall: Isaura, her son Tobiah and his daughter Linnet. Two are a pair in the sense of the Ladder, the dispatcher Dessa Varnholt and the brake inspector Rurik Sennet, who turn the two keys on the Fourth Line. One is a researcher, Dr. Calla Reth of Tarn House. The last two stand on either side of the water: Emeric Haldric, who commands it, and Jessamy Tolk, who steals it. Their arcs are set down below in the past tense, as the finished book will have them.

Isaura Ombrecht was sixty-one in Year one, Master Wright of the Greyfall yard, and the third generation of her family to braid sedgewire there. She had gone onto the long walks at fourteen, forty-seven years before Year one, and she had made or mended the rope on every line above Ketterby. She was broad, slow-spoken and nearly deaf in her left ear, which she put down to forty years of listening with the right. Her authority was the guild seal, a small brass stamp she pressed into the lead tag of each rope she certified, and for most of her life she used it as the Commission wished, certifying on schedule and grumbling in private. Her arc ran from obedience to refusal to inheritance. In Year three she would not certify ropes that the Commission had quietly stretched beyond seven years, and for that she lost her seal. By Year nine she had handed the yard to her granddaughter and taken the humblest post on the Ladder, Pass-keeper at Greyfall, where she laid a hand on a rope for one minute at a time and was, for the first time in her life, simply listening.

Her method was the book's account of craft. Isaura read a rope the way a doctor reads a wrist, with the flat of the fingers and no hurry, and she held that anything a hand could not feel was not worth worrying about, which was her great strength and her single blind spot. She had never learned to trust instruments, or other people's reports, or a young person's ear. Her pride was a physical thing, like her shoulders, and it cost her two years of a good relationship with her granddaughter before she understood what Linnet could do. Her private grief was her late husband, a rope-walker who fell from a scaffold at Cinder Rest when Tobiah was nine, an accident the Commission recorded as a fault in the scaffold and Isaura recorded, in a drawer, as a fault in the Commission. She spoke of him seldom. When she did it was usually to correct someone about the right way to lay a strand.

Tobiah Ombrecht was thirty-four in Year one, Isaura's only son and foreman of the Greyfall brake sheds. He kept the bands, drums and levers that stop the Great Sheave, and he was good at it in a way no one thanked him for, since a brake that works is invisible. He could tell from the smell of a drum how many weeks it had left, and he kept a notebook of smells that nobody was allowed to read. He loved the Great Sheave the way other men love a horse, and talked to it, quietly, when he thought the shed was empty. He was also, on the evidence of the yard, the only man in Greyfall who could make Isaura laugh. He was a widower, a gambler in a small and cautious way, and the father of Linnet, whom he raised mostly by leaving the door open. His debts were modest but real, and they were the lever by which Jessamy Tolk moved him. He had wanted to be a wright like his mother and had failed the ear test at sixteen, a humiliation he never named; his daughter passed it at fifteen without noticing it was a test. His was the book's slowest fall and its quietest recovery. In Year five he took the Syndicate's retainer to look away from the Held Minute. In Year eight he was the man who barred the door of his own brake house against a ghost run, and he ended the book with a limp, a clean ledger and a seat on the committee that wrote the new rules.

Linnet Ombrecht was fifteen in Year one, Tobiah's daughter and Isaura's granddaughter, and the one character the book lets change completely. She began as an apprentice assigned to the dullest job in the yard, counting the strands of a braided rope against its tag, and she was restless, quick, perpetually chewing the end of her braid, and rude to her elders in a way the yard forgave only because she was usually right. Her gift was her ear. Where her grandmother read a rope by hand, Linnet heard it: she could tell a sound rope from a dry one at forty paces by the note it gave off in wind, a thin steady hum for a healthy rope and a flatter, woollier sound when the sedge heart was drying. The yard called it the Ombrecht note, and in three generations nobody but she had inherited it. Isaura's first lesson, and the only advice of hers the book quotes, was short. "Do not look at the rope," she told the girl. "Listen to it."

Her arc was a ladder of its own, and it climbed in rungs the book can count. In Year three, when her grandmother lost the seal, Linnet became Isaura's ears in the plainest sense, walking the lines beside her and saying aloud what each rope was saying. In Year four she heard the Second Line's rope going flat and forced the question that finally mattered, whether a rope that the Commission's examiner had passed was still a rope. In Year seven she stood in front of the Assembly of Stations at twenty-one, too young to be believed and too exact to be dismissed. By Year nine she was twenty-three and Chief Wright at Greyfall, the youngest the yard had ever had, and the person who braided the first rope of the shortened Ladder. She never forgave the Commission its one-sentence answer to the guild's rope test, which she chalked on the yard wall, and she kept the habit of writing on the inside of her wrist every promise an official made to her. The book is told mostly through her eyes, with Calla's, and her anger is its engine: she is the only person in Drevast who is angry about the right thing at the right size.

Dessa Varnholt was forty-one in Year one, dispatcher at Greyfall, and keeper of the Book. The Book was the dispatch ledger in which every run on the Fourth Line was entered with its time, its tallies and the level of the belly at the fill, and her handwriting in it was so regular that the Commission once used a page as a specimen. Her desk stood at the window that looked down the Fourth Line, and she was said to know the day's weather by the colour of the rope before the dawn bell had finished. She was precise, dry and funny, had never been late in her life, and counted, by her own admission, as a form of prayer. She and Rurik Sennet had turned keys together for ten years, and the book is organised around the day the two-key rule failed, when each trusted the other's key to be the one that mattered. On the morning of the runaway the fill gauge at Greyfall read ninety-eight, eight above the Mark, and she told herself it ran high; she wrote the word Mark in the Book anyway, because the queue was long and the gauge was old. Her arc was a long confession. She kept silent through the inquiry, copied the Commissioner's memo in Year five and sent it to the lowland press, a decision that cost her her post and, in Year seven, two months in a Commission cell. "I wrote Mark because the Book had a column for it," she said, in the first honest sentence she spoke on the subject.

Rurik Sennet was forty-seven in Year one, brake inspector at Greyfall and Dessa's partner at the second key. He was large, silent and ashamed by temperament, the kind of man who apologises to machinery. He had come to the Ladder from the lowland railways at twenty-five and never fully trusted anything that moved under its own weight, himself included. On the morning of the runaway, in the October of Year three, he inspected the brake band of the Fourth Line and passed it. He knew it was due for relining. The Commission's circular of that spring had lengthened the interval from fifty days to seventy-five, and the band stood at sixty-four. He turned his key. Everything in his arc followed from the arithmetic of that morning: sixty-four was less than seventy-five, the circular was lawful, and eleven people died anyway.

He never defended himself. He accepted a three-month suspension without comment, and then did something the book treats as a kind of sainthood and a kind of stupidity: he refused to ride a car again. For four years he walked. In Year seven he walked the whole way from Greyfall to Ostrel, three lines and nearly a thousand metres of climb, to give evidence to the Assembly in person. "I turned the key," he said. "Say it plainly." The Assembly did, which was the beginning of the end of the circular. He finished the book as the first Inspector of Inspectors, a post invented for him, in which he visited every brake house in the country and signed nothing at all.

Dr. Calla Reth was thirty-eight in Year one, the Commission's chief hydrographer, which was a grand title for a woman who lived at Tarn House with a stove, a rotating cast of assistants and a shelf of notebooks. She was the researcher of the book and its most exact mind. She had come to the Brimmer nine years before Year one to measure a lake, and had stayed to measure the glacier above it, driving marked stakes into the tongue of Old Mara every February and reading how far the ice had slipped past them. She was solitary, and she believed that a sentence without a number in it was a mood. Her method was slow and her conclusions were not: Old Mara was losing about a metre of thickness in each year she measured, and the loss was speeding up.

Her arc was the book's argument. In Year one she wrote a report predicting what the Brimmer would do, and the Commissioner shelved it. In Year six she published the same numbers under her own name in the lowland press, after the memo was leaked and the shelf no longer held. In between she was the only character who knew how bad it was, and the book spends several chapters inside the loneliness of that. She did not become a heroine. She became a calendar: the Low Day tables she drew up in Year seven were adopted by the Assembly in Year nine, and for the rest of the country's life the date of Low Day was not discovered but looked up. She never married, kept a hen at Tarn House for reasons she declined to give, and ended the book still measuring, which the writer regards as the happiest ending available to her.

Emeric Haldric was fifty-eight in Year one, Commissioner of the HWC and the book's nearest thing to an antagonist, though the book works hard to deny him the title. He had been a bridge engineer before he was an official, and by the time the story opens he had held the Commissioner's seal for fourteen years and been reappointed once. He believed, with an engineer's sincerity, that the Ladder was the only thing standing between Drevast and the dark. He was orderly, tired and quotable, and he drank his tea cold on principle. His case was a serious one: a country told on a Tuesday that its water will fail in nine years will behave worse for those nine years than a country told nothing. So he told it nothing, and managed. His circulars were famous for their calm. His arc was a slow exposure, ending in Year seven with a resignation letter that he wrote in his own hand, a gesture the Assembly found more insulting than silence. One sentence of his was repeated in every account of his fall: "A frightened valley eats more than a hungry one."

Jessamy Tolk was forty-four in Year one, the Syndicate's night broker and the book's most likeable liar. She grew up on the Sill barges and had the lowlander's contempt for anyone who lived above the cloud. Her work was to find water, a hold and a pair of hands that would not ask, and she did all three with charm, tipping every weigher she met as a form of insurance. She kept a notebook of other people's debts, which she called her library, and she had never been seen to open it. She was not a villain by her own account. She argued that the Commission rationed water to keep prices high in Ostrel, that the Syndicate's ghost cars fed the valley better than the Weight Cuts, as the rationing was called, ever did, and that "water doesn't know whose it is". In places the book lets her be right. Her arc was a mirror of Haldric's: both were managers of scarcity, one by law and one by nerve. After the Reconciliation, the settlement of Year nine, she was folded into the Commission as Night Warden of the Ladder, a post she accepted with perfect and visible amusement, and the first thing she did in it was to close, with her own hands, the thief-pipes she had paid for.

Year one, February. Calla Reth drove her annual stakes into the tongue of Old Mara and found, within the hour, that the ice had slipped past the last row by almost twice the usual distance. She did not believe it, so she drove a spare row and measured again, and the spare agreed. That night she wrote nothing in the Commission's journal and everything in her own notebook, in pencil, with a question mark after the most important line. The novel opens here, on a sheet of blue ice with a woman kneeling on it, because its first task is to show that the shortage began as a number before it became a hunger. Over the spring she remeasured three times and drew a curve, and it was not a slope but a lip, the first edge of something that would fall away. She said so to nobody for nine months, which is the length of the first act.

Year one, May. Jessamy Tolk climbed to Greyfall on a day car and took a seat in the corner of the brake shed where the foreman kept a kettle. She asked Tobiah for nothing. She lent him two weeks' wages against a card debt, admired his bands, and left on the evening run, and he understood only later that he had been shown, politely, the size of the hole he would one day have to fill. The same night Linnet, who could not sleep and had taken to sitting on the yard roof, watched a car with no lamps slide down the black track of the Fourth Line and halt at the Pass for no minute at all. It was the first ghost car in the book. She told her grandmother, who told her to go to bed, and she told her father, who told her it was probably a lamp on the scree, and the fact that two adults she trusted lied to her in the same week is the root of everything she does later.

Year one, September. Low Day fell on the twenty-fourth, the earliest in the Commission's records. The Brimmer figure sank so far that the First Line managed only nineteen runs in a day when the ledgers promised twenty-three, and in Pannock a sack of barley meal that had cost four coppers in June cost seven. In the same week Linnet was formally apprenticed to her grandmother, a year later than the custom because Tobiah had delayed it, and was handed her first task: to count the strands in a sample rope against its tag until she could do it in the dark. She did it in the dark in nine days. Isaura, who had expected a month, said nothing, which in her was a form of applause. The book sets the two side by side: a girl learning to count rope while the country, a little further up the hill, learns to count water.

Year two, March. The Commissioner issued two circulars in a single week. The first, the Weight Cuts, reduced the permitted runs on every line by a sixth, so that a line which had managed thirty now managed twenty-five, and it was posted in every station under the heading of a seasonal adjustment. The second said that brake bands might run seventy-five days between relinings instead of fifty. The reasoning was sober. A relining took a line out of service for two days, two idle days on the lower lines were worth more than the small extra risk, and the water allocated to a stopped line simply ran away to the Sill unused. Nobody in the Commission thought the second circular was dangerous, and nobody in the field thought it was safe, and the difference between those two beliefs is the gap in which eleven people later died. Dessa pinned both circulars to the dispatch-room wall and, uncharacteristically, did not straighten the second.

Year two, October. On Haul Day, the first of the month, the Fourth Line ran away. The book gives the sequence in seven steps and never shows it all at once. First, the freight queue at Greyfall was the longest of the year, because the Weight Cuts had pushed September's barley into October. Second, Syndicate hands working the night shift had left the thief-pipe at Greyfall unplugged and a bung loose, so the cistern kept filling the waiting belly after the dawn fill had ended. Third, the fill gauge on that belly stuck at ninety-eight, and the belly went on filling to a hundred and eighteen barrels, twenty-eight over the Mark. Fourth, Dessa read ninety-eight, wrote Mark in the Book and turned her key; Rurik passed the brake band at sixty-four days and turned his; the two keys turned in the same minute, as the rule required. Fifth, the heavy car started down with a counterpoise far too large, and the brake band, working harder than it was built to, heated, glazed and lost its grip. Sixth, the cars reached the Pass without being able to stop, so the Held Minute never happened, and the descending car ran on to the foot of the line at Ketterby, where it struck the buffers, while the rising car was flung into the top of the station at Greyfall. Seventh, eleven people were dead, seven in the falling car and four in the rising one, in less than three minutes.

Year two, December. The inquiry sat for nine days in the hall of the dispatch school at Greyfall. It found a failure of a single fill gauge and a misreading by an experienced operator, suspended Rurik Sennet for three months, named two Syndicate hands who were never found, and ordered the thief-pipe at Greyfall to be filled with stone. It said nothing about the circular, the Weight Cuts, the queue, or the water the Syndicate had learned to take. Days after the report, the Commissioner issued a third circular, the Extension Order, which raised the working life of a haul-rope from seven years to nine on the grounds of a sedge blight. The blight was real. So was the rule it overrode. Isaura read the order standing up in the long walk and put it in the pocket where she kept her unlit pipe.

Year three, February. The Second Line's rope reached its seventh winter, and the Commission's examiner arrived at Greyfall with a lead tag and a request that Isaura certify it for two more years under the Extension Order. She declined. She said, correctly, that the guild's seal meant seven, and that she would not press her stamp into a lie to save a Commissioner a month's bread. The examiner, a polite young man with clean boots, said that the Commission would certify the rope itself. Isaura replied that it was welcome to, and could use its own tag. The exchange is the moment at which the country's one fully trusted craft begins to split from the institution that depends on it, and Isaura does not yet know she has done anything but be stubborn.

Year three, May. The guild, which owed the Commission a contract and a pension fund, withdrew Isaura's seal on a vote of fourteen to nine. She was not disgraced, exactly. She was asked to stay on as a senior hand at the same wage and to refrain from certifying, a courtesy that did more damage than a public rebuke would have. The yard went quiet around her. Within a week Linnet did what no one had suggested: she took her grandmother on a round of the lines, riding out to the Passes with a wright's pass and standing on the service ledge for the Held Minute, and told her, rope by rope, what she could hear. Isaura listened to the girl listening, and for the first time asked a question instead of giving a lesson. The book treats this as the real beginning of the Ombrecht craft, which is not a family trade handed down but a pair of ears and a pair of hands that learn to work as one.

Year three, August. Low Day fell on the twenty-seventh, four weeks earlier than in Year one, and Emeric Haldric climbed to Tarn House unannounced to see the lake for himself. He asked Calla whether the numbers were still the numbers. She said that they were. He asked, very quietly, whether she had told anyone, and she said that she had told the Commission, in a report, in Year one, which was where she had left it. He thanked her, which she had not expected, and went back down the lake path in the dusk. The scene is the only one in the book in which the two of them are alone together, and the writer wants it played with no villainy in it at all.

Year four, March. Linnet heard the Second Line's rope go flat. On the service ledge at the Pass, in a north wind, the note that had been steady in January had thinned and become woollen, the sound of a sedge heart drying. She told Isaura, who laid a hand on the rope, felt nothing wrong, and believed the girl anyway. The guild asked for a load test. The Commission's examiner refused it, and the rope kept working. A month later the guild tested a spare length cut from the same braiding, and the sample lost a fifth of its strength between the first pull and the fifth. The Commission's reply was a single sentence: guild tests of spare lengths were not evidence about rope in service. Linnet wrote it on the yard wall in chalk, and it stayed there for three winters.

Year four, November. The Commissioner sent a confidential memorandum to the chiefs of all eight stations, and Dessa Varnholt, who as dispatcher at Greyfall was entitled to see her chief's mail, read it twice before putting it back in the tray. The Assembly was due to debate the Weight Cuts in the new year, the Pannock press had begun to ask about the glacier, and the memo was Haldric's attempt to give every station chief the same sentence to say. He wrote it himself, at night, with the door shut, in the hand he used for things he did not want typed. It is set down here almost whole, because the book quotes it and because the writer wants its voice to be heard against everything around it: a flat, passive, official voice, in which nobody does anything and everything is merely noted. The memorandum runs as follows.

Confidential. To the Station Chiefs of the Ladder, from the Office of the Commissioner, on the subject of seasonal draw. It is the view of this Office that the present pattern of delivery from the Brimmer lies within the range of variation that may reasonably be anticipated in a mountain catchment and does not at this time warrant any departure from established practice. Station Chiefs are accordingly reminded that figures relating to the retreat of Old Mara, whether prepared by Commission staff or by other parties, remain the property of the Commission and are not to be circulated, discussed in public houses, or conveyed to the press. Where enquiries are received, the approved form of reply is that the Commission monitors the glacier closely and is satisfied. It is further noted that the reduction of the permitted draw during the Thin Season is to be described in local notices as a seasonal adjustment and not as a reduction. Chiefs are asked to bear in mind that an adjustment may be reversed, whereas a reduction may not.

With regard to the extension of rope life announced two winters ago, Chiefs will note that ropes between seven and nine years of age are to be certified on the strength of the Commission's own examiner and not of the guild, whose reservations, though noted with respect, are considered to be of a commercial character. With regard to brake bands, the interval of seventy-five days remains in force. Chiefs are reminded that the interval is a maximum, and that nothing in this Office's circular should be read as discouraging earlier relining where it can be arranged without loss of draw. This Office is aware that the foregoing places a considerable burden of judgment on those in the field, and wishes it recorded that such judgment is valued. Should difficulty arise, Chiefs will wish to be certain that the record of their instructions is clear. This memorandum is not to be copied.

Year five, July. Tobiah Ombrecht took the Syndicate's retainer. The sum was forty crowns a quarter, which was a little less than he owed and a great deal more than he earned, and what it bought was small and exact: on certain nights, on the Fourth Line, a brake shed that was shut and a foreman who was not at his post. He told himself that a ghost car was only a run, and that he was moving a few barrels of grain for people who were hungry. He told himself so on the walk home and again the next morning, and Linnet, who had learned to read her father's silences the way she read ropes, heard the change in him within a week. The book keeps this decision very small. There is no scene in which anyone offers him a bag of money. There is a kettle, a card game, a pause in a conversation, and a man who wanted, more than he wanted to be good, to stop owing.

Year five, November. Dessa Varnholt copied the memo by hand at the dispatch desk, in her regular and unmistakable writing, and posted it to the editor of the Sill Evening Post in Pannock. She did not sign it. She did not need to; the Commission identified the hand within a week. The leak caused no scandal. It caused something worse for Haldric, a long run of small questions: why a station chief had been told what to say about a glacier, who the examiner was whose judgment replaced the guild's, what a reduction was if it was not an adjustment. She was relieved of the Book in December and kept on at half wages in the signal room, where for the better part of two years she transmitted other people's figures without comment.

Year six, April. Calla Reth's paper, On the Retreat of Old Mara, appeared in three issues of the Sill Evening Post, and it was the first time anyone in the lowlands had seen the glacier's numbers set down plainly: the thickness of the ice, the curve through it, and a table of dates. The table's last column named the day on which the Brimmer would reach its lowest figure, the sixteenth of July. The Commission replied that the paper was the work of an individual and did not reflect the position of the HWC. Calla's letter to the editor was the shortest thing she ever wrote for publication: wait until July. The Assembly questioned Haldric in June, and he attended in a clean collar and answered every question in complete sentences.

Year six, July. Low Day fell on the sixteenth, as the table had said. The Brimmer figure was the lowest in the Commission's records by a margin that the gauge-keeper at Tarn House, who had read it for thirty years, described as indecent, and the First Line managed fourteen runs in a day for the first time. In Pannock, bread went to a price at which grown men queued with a handful of coins and a stunned look. The prediction had been exact to the day, and nothing that Haldric had said in June could be unsaid. It is the first part of the book in which the shortage stops being an opinion. Yet the Assembly did not act. A sitting body that has been proved wrong about the past tends to ask for more time to examine the future, and it voted in July to commission a study.

Year one, November. Here the timeline of the bible jumps backward five years, because the book interrupts its own order to go back to the report that Haldric shelved, so that the reader reads it only after July has proved it right. Calla took her stakes, her curve and a three-page argument to the Commissioner's office. She calculated that Old Mara had lost better than nine metres of thickness since her first stake, and that the Brimmer, which holds sixty thousand barrels when full, would be refilled each year by a glacier that delivered less and earlier, so that Low Day would not stay in September; it would walk backward through the summer by roughly a fortnight a year. She asked for two things: to publish, and to begin planning for a Ladder that ran on less. Haldric read the report standing and said that it was admirable and that it would be filed under Prudence. He said that publication would cause the very harm that planning was meant to avoid. He said it kindly. She walked back up to Tarn House by the lake path, and the gate-weigher, who did not know her errand, remarked that she looked like a woman who had seen the end of something. She had. She just did not yet have a date for it.

Year seven, February. The Assembly of Stations reopened the inquiry into the Fourth Line. Rurik Sennet, who had not ridden in a car since the runaway, set out from Greyfall on foot in a Thin Season gale, walking the stair-paths beside the Fifth, Sixth and Seventh lines for nine days and sleeping in the Pass-keepers' huts, whose keepers gave him tea and said nothing. He arrived at Ostrel with a swollen ankle and was admitted to the hall on a Tuesday. Linnet and Isaura had come up the Ladder by car two days earlier, and Linnet gave her evidence about the Second Line's rope first, in a voice that did not shake. Rurik gave his second. He had prepared four sentences and said three of them before the chair interrupted to ask whether he understood what he was admitting. "I turned the key," he said. "Say it plainly." The hall was silent, and then a man at the back began, with a kind of horror, to write.

Year seven, September. Emeric Haldric resigned. The Assembly had voted in August to receive Calla's tables, to end the brake-interval circular and the Extension Order, and to audit the water taken by ghost cars; Haldric read the three decisions, took a sheet of paper, and wrote his letter by hand. It was a good letter. It said that he had acted at all times in the interest of the country, that he regretted nothing he had done, and that he regretted several things he had not. The Assembly found it more insulting than silence, which is what the book intends. On his last morning he walked the length of the weighing hall at Ostrel, stepped onto the gate scales and had himself weighed like any passenger, and the weigher, who had chalked his figure on that wall for as long as anyone could remember, wrote it up without a word, which was his own kind of salute. He went down to Pannock by car, paying his fare by the tally, and he was lighter, the weigher noted privately, than on the day he took the seal. Dessa Varnholt was released from the Commission cell on the same day, after two months, and walked out into the high pale light of Ostrel carrying a ledger she had been forbidden to bring in. The ledger was blank. She had kept it ruled for two months in case she was ever asked to write something down.

Year eight, January. At two in the morning, on the coldest night of the Thin Season, three Syndicate hands came to the brake house at Greyfall to run a ghost car down the Fourth Line. They had a key, a bung and a story, and they expected, from experience, a foreman who was not at his post. Tobiah Ombrecht was at his post. He had stopped taking the retainer, with no ceremony, in the autumn of Year seven, and he had been sleeping in the brake house since, on a cot beside the levers. He barred the door from inside. The hands broke the latch, and he stood in front of the Sheave brake with his arms across it. "The key is in my pocket," he said, "and my pocket is staying where it is." They beat him, without any particular malice, and broke his knee, and Linnet, arriving on the run from the yard with a lantern, found her father on the floor, laughing in pain, with the brake still locked.

Year nine, June. Low Day fell on the fourth, in the middle of the Fill Season, which no one alive had thought possible, though Calla's table had said so a year earlier. On the ninth the Brimmer figure sank below the line at which a single belly could be filled and still leave the Sluice anything to pass, and the Seventh Line stopped, for the first time since it opened. The Sixth followed two days later and the Fifth after that. Within a week the whole Ladder above Ketterby was silent, and the cars stood in their stations like houses. Ostrel woke to a quiet it had never known: no bells, no rattle, no chalk on the weigher's wall. The Lid had become a lid. People came into the square and stood about. Down at Greyfall, Isaura laid a hand on the stopped rope in the Pass and, for the first time in her life, felt nothing at all, and said what everyone had been waiting for someone to say: the rope was not broken, the water was gone. The next morning the Assembly met in the open air.

Year nine, August. The Reconciliation was signed at Ostrel on a table carried out of the Commission's grey building, and its terms are the book's ending. The Ladder was shortened and given a calendar. The Ketterby Cut, a feeder channel that brought the springs of the eastern pastures to the top of the Third Line, was dug over the two summers that followed, so that the Third, Second and First Lines could run all year on water that did not come from Old Mara. The four lines above it, the Fourth to the Seventh, became the Summer Ladder, which ran for sixteen weeks of the Fill Season on the dates in Calla's Low Day tables, and slept the rest. The Commission was reformed as a council with a seat for the wrights and a seat for the Syndicate. Dessa was pardoned, Rurik became Inspector of Inspectors, Jessamy Tolk became Night Warden, Isaura went to the Pass, and Linnet became Chief Wright and braided the first rope of the Summer Ladder in the Thin Season that followed. Ostrel lost a third of its people within four years, and the Lid learned to grow barley under glass. The book ends on the first morning of the first Summer Ladder, with Linnet on the service ledge at the Pass, in the Held Minute, listening.

The novel itself is told in close third person and in the past tense, alternating between Linnet and Calla, and each of its chapters opens with a weight: a number of tallies, a number of barrels, a reading from the gauge-post. It has thirty chapters in three movements. The first, up to the runaway, teaches the reader how the Ladder works and lets them love it. The second, up to the leak, shows what it costs to keep the Ladder running as it was. The third, up to the end, is the shortest, and it is mostly people standing in rooms and agreeing, with great politeness, to be smaller. The writer wants the prose to be as dry as the Commission's ledgers and as exact as Calla's notebooks, with feeling allowed only in what people do with their hands. There is little dialogue, because the people of Drevast say less than they know, and where it appears it is short and it is usually an admission. This bible keeps to the same habits. It is in the third person throughout, it speaks in the past tense about what happens in the book, and it slips into the present tense, without apology, whenever it explains how the Ladder, the Commission or the water works, because those things stay true for as long as the book is being read.

The book is not a disaster story, and the writer should resist every temptation to give it one, however small. There is no flood, no burst dam, no riot in the square, and no villain with a plan. Its subject is how decent institutions fail by degrees, one lawful step at a time: the circular that is lawful, the key that is turned because the other key was turned, the report that is filed under Prudence. Three motifs recur, and none of them is explained to the reader. The first is listening, in the Held Minute, in Linnet's ear and in Isaura's hand on the rope. The second is counting, in the Book, in the tallies and in Calla's notebooks. The third is the word Mark, which begins as a ring of paint inside a tank, becomes a lie in a ledger, and ends as a promise. The title belongs to the same family. A counterpoise is a weight that balances another weight, and the book asks what it costs a country to keep one side of the balance a secret from the people standing on the other.

A few things stay deliberately undecided. The book never says whether the Ketterby Cut will last, or whether the Summer Ladder is the end of the Ladder or only its next form. It does not say who owned the thief-pipe at Greyfall on the night of the runaway, because the Syndicate's hands were never found and Jessamy Tolk, asked directly, only repeats her favourite sentence. And it never settles whether the Commission, had Haldric published Calla's report in Year one, could have saved anything. Calla thinks so. Haldric does not. Linnet says it does not matter, since the rope was already flat. The writer is content to leave all three open, because a bible that answers every question tends to produce a novel that does the same.
